title: POC scoping: cost modeling with Orchid AI
summary: Initial POC scoping to align on success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, and cost model. Customer wants to validate latency and per-token economics for a recommendation/chat feature under a constrained budget. Redwood AE+SE outlined batching, caching, quantization levers and proposed a 4-week POC with benchmarks and cost estimates.

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we scheduled 55 minutes. quick intros?
[00:08] Maya: hi maya here, head of ML at Orchid, we've been prototyping recommendation chat and want to scope a POC for production inference.
[00:16] Lucas: lucas, platform engineering, i'll be responsible for infra and networking.
[00:19] Sofia: sofia, cto, i'll jump in on questions about budget and timelines.
[00:25] Jordan: great, from Redwood we have priya (se) and marco on solutions. goal today is to align success criteria, workload size, and do cost modeling so we know if the POC fits your budget. sound right?
[00:36] Maya: yes, main success criteria are 1) p95 latency under 300ms for interactive flows, 2) model quality parity with our current fine-tuned LLM (we'll share eval set), and 3) keep monthly inference cost under roughly $25k for the pilot.
[00:50] Priya: ok perfect. quick clarifying Qs on workload: what’s your expected qps and average tokens/input+output for the pilot?
[00:58] Maya: for the pilot we expect sustained 5 qps with bursts to 20 for short windows. avg tokens per request is about 350 input and 120 output, so call it ~470 tokens.
[01:12] Jordan: thanks — we'll use 500 tokens/request as a working number so margins are easier. with 5 qps that works out to ~6.48 billion tokens/month if sustained 24/7, but pilots are usually smaller in duration, still good to size.
[01:28] Sofia: that token math sounds big, is that monthly? our budget numbers assume lower effective usage because not all users are hitting the model constantly.
[01:36] Marco: right — two levers to reduce cost: batching (increase throughput efficiency) and prefix/KV caching to avoid re-computation for repeated contexts, plus quantization to cut model compute.
[01:46] Lucas: curious — what's the delta between hosted API and dedicated in unit economics? we need to know if Dedicated reserved capacity is necessary for latency/SLA.
[01:55] Priya: good question. rough ballpark: hosted (shared) runtimes with our curated model run you roughly $0.00003 per token baseline, with batching/caching that can get to $0.00001 per token in some workloads. Dedicated can reduce variability and sometimes reduces marginal cost if you commit, but has a fixed monthly reserved capacity fee.
[02:14] Maya: wait to confirm — $0.00003/token is about $30 per million tokens?
[02:18] Jordan: yes, exactly — $30 per 1M tokens baseline. at 6.5B tokens that would be ~195k/month without optimizations, so the goal is to use batching/caching/quantization to meet your $25k pilot budget.
[02:33] Sofia: ok that's helpful, what are realistic optimizations we should expect for our workload?
[02:38] Priya: typical wins: batching (x2-x3 token efficiency depending on prompt lengths), prefix caching (if you have repeated system prompts or user context, cache hit rate could cut calls by 20-40%), and quantized model variants (4-bit) can reduce GPU cost ~30-50% depending on the kernel. combined we often see 3-8x reduction vs naive baseline.
[02:59] Lucas: so if we assume 4x reduction and $30/1M baseline, that puts us at ~$7.5/1M effectively? math check.
[03:06] Jordan: roughly yes — $30/1M divided by 4 becomes $7.5/1M, so your 6.5B tokens would be ~48,750 (= 6,480M /1M * $7.5 = $48,600) — still over your $25k, but remember pilots are smaller traffic or you can limit concurrency and sample traffic.
[03:23] Maya: for the pilot we can cap usage to office hours and run a subset of users, do you have an example POC plan?
[03:29] Marco: we propose a 4-week POC: week1 ingest sample prompts & traffic (you share), week2 baseline hosted runs with full-precision model to measure quality and latency, week3 run quantized + batching + caching profiles, week4 reliability tests and cost runups. We'll provide a cost workbook with scenarios: hosted baseline, hosted optimized, dedicated (1-month commit) optimized.
[03:50] Sofia: timeline seems reasonable. what's in the cost workbook?
[03:54] Jordan: workbook has per-token assumptions, batching factors, cache hit rates, estimated compute hours, Dedicated reserved cost line items, and a summary metric: estimated $/1M tokens and projected monthly cost at your expected QPS profile.
[04:07] Lucas: on networking, we will likely run in our VPC for the POC. how does Redwood handle private deployment / VPC peering?
[04:14] Priya: Redwood Private supports VPC peering and we can do a controlled setup; for the pilot we can use a secure tunnel or dedicated peering. we'll need egress rules and a short list of IPs. also we support KMS for key management for any logs or encryption needs.
[04:29] Maya: SOC2 and audit logs matter for us — we need to see retention policy and access logs.
[04:33] Jordan: we'll include our security pack (SOC 2 summary, SAML/SSO guides, audit log docs) in the follow-up.
[04:39] Maya: thanks. for quality gates, we'll validate using your eval harness?
[04:43] Priya: yes we have an eval harness and can run your test set automatically and report BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics or direct human eval comparisons. we'll flag regressions against your fine-tuned baseline.
[04:52] Lucas: benchmarks: what exact tests will you run for latency/throughput?
[04:56] Marco: plan: 1) single request p95/p99 latency with cold KV cache, 2) sustained qps soak at your target 5 qps and burst tests to 20 qps to measure autoscale and tail latency, and 3) mixing quantized model throughput (4-bit) vs fp16. We'll do both hosted and dedicated nodes if you want to compare.
[05:18] Maya: how many synthetic queries do you need from us?
[05:21] Priya: 5-10k representative queries for bench runs; if you can share 2 weeks of telemetry that helps us model real hit rates and concurrency.
[05:29] Jordan: about benchmarks, one nuance: batching helps throughput but can increase latency tail for single interactive calls unless we use adaptive batching windows — we can tune that per-route.
[05:40] Sofia: we're sensitive to p95 tails; interactive users will churn if latency spikes.
[05:44] Priya: understood — our tuning knobs: max batch size, batching timeout (we've seen 10-30ms window tradeoffs), and smart routing to prefer low-latency nodes for interactive traffic. Also KV prefix caching can make responses near instant for repeated contexts.
[05:58] Lucas: anything else on cost modeling assumptions?
[06:01] Jordan: we'll include assumptions as clearly labeled cells: avg tokens per request, qps profile, hit rate assumptions (e.g., 30% cache hit), batching factor (x2-3), quantization uplift. We'll show low/median/high scenarios.
[06:14] Maya: good. can you provide a sample math example on the call?
[06:18] Jordan: sure — take your pilot profile: 5 qps sustained, 500 tokens/request, 30 days. naive tokens/month = 5 * 2,592,000 * 500 = 6,480,000,000 tokens = 6,480M. baseline $30/1M -> $194,400/month. With 4x overall optimization -> effective $7.5/1M -> $48,600/month. If you limit active hours to 10 hours/day average usage and sample users (reduces by ~60%) -> down to ~$19k/month, which fits your $25k pilot target.
[06:51] Sofia: interesting — so operational controls + optimizations are key.
[06:56] Maya: what about canarying and rollbacks in the POC? we need safety nets.
[07:00] Marco: we support route-level rollouts, canary percentages, and automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant if latency or error rate exceeds thresholds. We'll include that in the runbook.
[07:12] Lucas: for Dedicated, what's the minimum commit?
[07:15] Jordan: Dedicated typically has monthly reserved nodes; pricing depends on GPU type and count — in the workbook we'll show a small Dedicated cluster option (1-2 GPUs) and amortize commit vs variable hosted cost. Sometimes the commit only makes sense if you cross tens of billions of tokens/month.
[07:30] Priya: one more thing on benchmarking: we might instrument token-level cost and break down latency per kernel (attn vs kv). that helps prioritize where quantization helps most.
[07:40] Maya: great. on timeline — can we kick off next week?
[07:43] Jordan: yes — if you can share sample prompts by 2026-07-01 we'll start baseline tests week of 2026-07-06. propose a 4-week cadence ending 2026-07-31 with a final review and recommendation.
[07:55] Sofia: ok that works. any blockers we haven't covered?
[07:59] Lucas: networking details and IP allowlist; we'll validate with security team.
[08:03] Jordan: action items recap: we'll send the workbook and security pack; you send telemetry and prompts; schedule bench kick-off.
[08:11] Maya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:14] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up with concrete dates and the workbook.
[08:20] Speaker 1: meeting ended

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., Redwood product names appear as Redwood "Dediated" in the auto transcript), timestamps are approximated every ~30-60 seconds. The dialogue includes natural hesitations and overlapping talk where indicated.

Bench plan (short):
- 10k synthetic queries + 2 weeks prod telemetry to model cache hit rate and concurrency
- Run hosted baseline (fp16) -> record p95/p99 latencies, token throughput
- Run quantized 4-bit variant with batching profiles (batch sizes 4, 8, 16) -> compare throughput and quality
- Run dedicated small cluster (if requested) to compare variability and unit cost
- Produce cost workbook with low/median/high scenarios and recommended knobs to meet $25k pilot target

Common glossary/assumptions used:
- Token estimate: 500 tokens/request (350 in, 150 out)
- Conservative cache hit rate for planning: 20-30%
- Batching factor: 2-3x typical for 500-token avg prompts
- Quantization uplift: 30-50% compute reduction depending on model/ops

End of transcript.
